sections.Introduction:
The human brain differs from other organs because it receives a complex vascular supply through an intricate arterial network. The cerebral vascular supply is divided into the anterior and posterior circulations. The internal carotid arteries (ICAs) are the primary contributors to the anterior circulation, whereas the vertebral arteries are the primary contributors to the posterior circulation.

Important branches arise as the ICA courses superiorly, including the posterior communicating (PCom), anterior choroidal (AChA), anterior cerebral (ACA), and middle cerebral (MCA) arteries. The terminal ICAs, ACAs, anterior communicating artery, PComs, and posterior cerebral arteries (PCAs) form the circle of Willis, which provides potential collateral flow between the anterior and posterior circulations. This collateral pathway may preserve cerebral perfusion when a major supplying artery becomes stenosed or occluded (see Image. Brain Blood Circulation). Although major ICA branches, such as the ACA and MCA, supply extensive territories of the cerebral hemispheres, smaller-caliber branches, such as the AChA, also play essential functional roles.

Isolated AChA territory infarction is uncommon, though the artery may be involved in ischemic stroke, aneurysms, arteriovenous malformations (AVMs), moyamoya disease, and intracranial tumors. Knowledge of AChA anatomy and vascular territory is essential for accurate diagnosis, surgical planning, and interpretation of neuroimaging findings.
sections.Structure and Function:
The AChA is the last major branch of the ICA before its bifurcation and supplies several critical brain structures involved in vision and motor function. The AChA arises from the posterior wall of the ICA and most commonly originates 2 to 5 mm distal to the PCom.[1][2]

The AChA courses posteriorly in close relation to the optic tract and uncus before entering the temporal horn through the choroidal fissure at the inferior choroidal, or plexal, point. The segment extending from the origin to the choroidal fissure is known as the cisternal segment, which is divided at the arterial genu into preoptic and postoptic portions. The postoptic portion is longer and generally gives rise to more perforating branches supplying critical deep structures. This subdivision helps anticipate the location of perforating branches during surgery. Beyond the plexal point, the AChA continues as the plexal, or intraventricular, segment, supplying the choroid plexus of the temporal horn and forming anastomoses with the posterior choroidal branches.

Throughout the cisternal segment, the AChA supplies variable portions of the posterior limb and retrolenticular part of the internal capsule, optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, and cerebral peduncle.[3] The posterior limb of the internal capsule contains corticospinal, corticobulbar, and thalamocortical fibers. The optic tract and lateral geniculate nucleus relay visual information, and ischemia within the AChA territory may produce visual field deficits. Despite its small caliber, the AChA gives rise to perforating branches that supply the medial segment of the globus pallidus, portions of the amygdala and hippocampus, and regions of the substantia nigra and red nucleus.
sections.Surgical Considerations: The AChA gives rise to multiple perforating branches that supply critical brain structures. Adjunctive measures should be used during surgical clipping of AChA aneurysms whenever possible. Vascular patency should be assessed with direct microscopic inspection, indocyanine green videoangiography, microvascular Doppler ultrasonography, and, when findings remain uncertain, intraoperative digital subtraction angiography. Neurophysiologic monitoring with motor-evoked potentials, with or without somatosensory evoked potentials, is also recommended. These adjuncts complement, but do not replace, direct microscopic inspection because delayed arterial occlusion, kinking, or flow insufficiency may occur despite apparently preserved fluorescence or Doppler flow.[8]
sections.Clinical Significance:
Aneurysms

Aneurysms are the most common lesions involving the AChA. Although only 2% to 4% of all intracranial aneurysms arise from this blood vessel, recognition of the clinical features is essential for diagnosis. Risk factors for AChA aneurysms are similar to those for intracranial aneurysms elsewhere and include autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, connective tissue disorders like Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, advanced age, smoking, and hypertension. AChA aneurysms may be discovered incidentally or present after rupture with subarachnoid hemorrhage. Rupture may occur even in relatively small AChA aneurysms, although current evidence is limited, and treatment decisions should not be based on aneurysm size alone.

Treatment should be individualized according to rupture status, aneurysm morphology, and AChA involvement. Available options include surgical clipping, endovascular coiling with or without adjunctive devices, and flow diversion in selected cases.[9][10] Treatment planning depends particularly on whether the AChA arises proximal to the aneurysm or is incorporated into the aneurysm neck or sac because arterial incorporation increases the risk of treatment-related occlusion and ischemic injury. Selected small, unruptured AChA aneurysms may be managed conservatively with modification of vascular risk factors and regular imaging surveillance. Long-term follow-up is required after both microsurgical and endovascular treatment because neck remnants or recurrent aneurysms may enlarge and require retreatment, occasionally several years after the initial procedure.[11]

Arteriovenous Malformations

AVMs of the temporal horn or choroidal fissure may receive arterial supply from both the AChA and posterior choroidal arteries and typically drain through the deep venous system. Staged preoperative embolization may reduce nidus flow and venous hypertension in selected large, high-flow lesions, facilitating subsequent microsurgical resection and potentially reducing intraoperative blood loss. Management should be individualized according to angioarchitecture, nidus size, anatomic location, venous drainage, and relationships to critical structures. Embolization of AVMs through the AChA is technically demanding because the vessel may provide en-passage supply to eloquent structures. Superselective catheterization and careful assessment of normal perforating branches are essential.
